The research design is cross-sectional correlational study to collect data from university students aged from 18 to 23 years old. The sample size was 600 students taken via purposive sampling from the University of Gujrat, Pakistan. Standardized psychological scales of ChatGPT usage scale, critical thinking evaluation scale, and academic integrity scales were used. Our findings showed that ChatGPT has no significant effect on academic integrity but has positive effect on critical thinking. While critical thinking has positive effect on academic integrity. It showed that ChatGPT doesn’t directly change cheating behavior, but it can boost critical thinking for students, and that improved critical thinking is what increases academic integrity. Implications of the findings are discussed.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) writing companions are changing how second-language (L2) writers plan, formulate, and revise texts. Yet improved textual fluency does not necessarily indicate deeper learning or stronger independent writing ability. This conceptual article develops a framework for interpreting AI-assisted L2 writing through the Cognitive Process Model of Writing, Cognitive Load Theory, and the Output Hypothesis. It argues that AI assistance may redistribute rather than simply reduce cognitive effort: linguistic suggestions can ease some local formulation demands, while evaluating, adapting, and verifying generated language creates additional monitoring demands. Whether this redistribution supports learning depends on the learner’s agency, the transparency of the task, and the instructional design. The article proposes a three-phase pedagogical model: supported conceptual ideation, autonomous drafting, and collaborative critical revision. Across these phases, AI support is deliberately varied so that learners can benefit from assistance without surrendering authorship, monitoring, or opportunities for linguistic retrieval. The paper is conceptual and does not report an empirical experiment. It therefore offers propositions and a research agenda rather than claims of measured effects. The framework can guide future classroom research, instrument development, and responsible integration of generative AI into L2 writing curricula.

items.title: Transforming Science Education through Artificial Intelligence (AI): Opportunities, Challenges, and Implications for Students' Critical Thinking Skills in the Digital Era.
items.venue: Assoeltan Indonesian Journal of Community Research and Engagement

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping science education by expanding access to information, supporting adaptive instruction, enabling simulations, and providing timely feedback. This article examines the opportunities, challenges, and implications of AI integration for students’ critical thinking in the digital era. Using a narrative literature review, the study synthesizes foundational scholarship on AI in education, science learning, AI literacy, and critical thinking, alongside recent reviews and international guidance. The synthesis indicates that AI can support critical thinking when it is embedded in inquiry-oriented activities that require students to formulate questions, interpret scientific evidence, compare explanations, identify limitations, and justify conclusions. AI-supported simulations, conversational systems, and feedback tools may make abstract concepts more accessible and provide opportunities for iterative reasoning. However, these benefits are not automatic. Hallucinated information, algorithmic bias, privacy risks, unequal access, academic integrity concerns, and cognitive over-reliance may weaken learning if AI outputs are accepted without verification. The article argues that AI should function as a cognitive partner rather than a substitute for students’ intellectual work. Effective integration therefore requires scientific and AI literacy, teacher mediation, transparent assessment, ethical safeguards, and learning tasks that make reasoning visible. A human-centred approach can help science education use AI to strengthen, rather than displace, independent and evidence-based thinking.

items.title: Neural Mechanisms of Willed Attention Control

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Cueing paradigms are commonly used to study the neural mechanisms of visual spatial attention control. In these paradigms, each trial starts with an external cue, which instructs the subject to pay covert attention to a spatial location in anticipation of an impending stimulus (instructed attention). Recent work has introduced a new type of cue which prompts the subject to spontaneously decide which spatial location to attend (willed attention). We studied the neural mechanisms of willed attention control by analyzing fMRI and EEG data recorded at two institutions (UF and UC Davis) using the same willed attention paradigm. The findings include: (1) both instructional cues and the choice cue activated the DAN, (2) the choice cue additionally activated a frontoparietal decision network consisting of dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), anterior insula (AI), anterior prefrontal cortex (APFC), dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), and inferior parietal lobule (IPL), (3) the decision about where to attend can be decoded in frontoparietal decision network in choice trials but not in instructional trials, and (4) EEG alpha oscillation patterns immediately preceding the choice cue, but not the instructional cues, predicted the postcue direction of attention and the frontoparietal decision network activity. Based on these findings we proposed a model of willed attention control suggesting how the direction of visual spatial attention was decided upon in the absence of external instructions.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in language education, yet evidence from secondary-school settings remains fragmented. This integrative review examines empirical research on GenAI in formal secondary language education published from January 2023 to September 2026, with attention to pedagogical applications, language skills and activities, learning outcomes, teacher mediation, implementation challenges, and gaps in the evidence. Guided by Whittemore and Knafl’s integrative-review methodology and a PICo framework, the review drew on Google Scholar, ERIC, publisher and journal websites, and citation chasing. Twenty-two empirical studies were examined against the review criteria and available original publication records. Narrative and thematic synthesis were used to compare study contexts, methods, reported outcomes, and limitations. The studies describe uses of GenAI for writing support, feedback, conversation, tutoring, learning companionship, teacher support, and AI-literacy activities. Writing is the most represented language focus. Reported outcomes are mixed, ranging from gains in selected skills and learner perceptions to null or qualified findings. Overall, the evidence indicates that the educational contribution of GenAI depends on task design, teacher mediation, verification, AI literacy, and the conditions in which the technology is used.

quarantine.title: Generative AI use and scientific literacy among 15-year-olds in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, China: the mediating role of academic help-seeking

quarantine.abstract_text: Introduction Adolescents increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots for schoolwork, yet evidence on whether this use supports or undermines learning is mixed. Drawing on research on cognitive offloading and self-regulated learning, we examined whether GenAI use for schoolwork is related to scientific literacy directly and through two components of self-regulated learning, academic help-seeking and metacognitive strategy use, and whether the purpose of use matters. Methods We analyzed the Program for International Student Assessment 2025 (PISA 2025) data from 12,191 15-year-old students in 374 schools in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, China. Weighted two-level mediation models compared students within the same school, used all ten plausible values, and evaluated indirect effects with Monte Carlo confidence intervals. Results were checked against a design-based model with school fixed effects and balanced repeated replication weights. Results Students who used GenAI more often than their schoolmates reported more help-seeking ( β = 0.17) and more metacognitive strategy use ( β = 0.30). Help-seeking was positively associated with scientific literacy, yielding a positive indirect effect ( β = 0.013, 95% CI [0.009, 0.017]); the indirect effect through metacognitive strategies was smaller ( β = 0.007) and was fully accounted for by science self-efficacy. The direct association between GenAI use and scientific literacy was negative ( β = −0.048, about 4 PISA points), and the positive indirect effects offset about 40% of it, leaving a small negative total association ( β = −0.028). Purpose mattered: among users, using GenAI “to help me learn” was associated with higher scientific literacy (+5.8 points per response category), whereas using it to summarize texts, research new topics, or draft assignments was associated with lower scores (−6.6 points). The results did not differ by gender or socioeconomic status and were identical under the design-based model. Discussion GenAI use for schoolwork is associated with scientific literacy through opposing pathways: a positive one through academic help-seeking and a negative direct one, and the direction of the association differs by purpose of use. Because the data are cross-sectional, these associations may partly reflect which students use GenAI rather than the effects of its use.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Lexical errors are among the most frequent and persistent issues in second language (L2) production, yet research on vocabulary exercises has largely focused on the acquisition of new words rather than on the correction of misused ones. This exploratory repeated-measures study investigates the potential of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to provide personalized vocabulary practice targeting learner-specific lexical errors in Spanish. Eighty-five L2 and heritage learners across proficiency levels completed 15 individualized exercises generated by a custom GPT-based system from their own writing errors. The tasks varied in goal, format, linguistic complexity, and involvement load (IL). Error recognition and correction were assessed at immediate and delayed post-tests, and mixed-effects models showed that higher exercise performance and task-induced IL predicted better outcomes. Both recognition and correction declined at the delayed post-test, although only recognition did so significantly. Among exercise features, productive, contextualized formats such as text editing, translation, and sentence reconstruction showed strong positive associations with correction, while goals emphasizing paraphrastic flexibility were less favorable. At the learner level, outcomes also varied substantially. Overall, the findings suggest that GenAI can support scalable, individualized, error-driven vocabulary practice. Still, variability across learners and exercises, together with incomplete retention, indicates that personalization alone may not ensure durable learning. Future research should thus examine whether feedback, recycling, and adaptive review improve retention.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract This three‐level meta‐analysis examined when generative AI (GenAI) works for second language (L2) learning, synthesizing 67 effect sizes from 48 controlled studies ( N = 5196) published between 2023 and 2026, with a focus on GenAI's text generation and conversational interaction capabilities. GenAI demostrated a large overall effect on measured L2 learning outcomes ( g = 0.76, 95% CI [0.50, 1.02]); after removal of influential outliers, the effect remained significant but was smaller ( g = 0.57). Effects varied by skill domain: speaking showed the largest full‐sample effect ( g = 1.48), which declined substantially after outlier adjustment ( g = 0.65), while vocabulary ( g = 0.66) and writing ( g = 0.61) remained moderate and reading was non‐significant. Regarding integration design, GenAI functioning as a feedback and assessment provider yielded the largest effects (full‐sample g = 1.15; adjusted g = 0.83), and interaction configurations with higher learner agency (Student‐Led, g = 0.92; Co‐Creative, g = 0.82) outperformed AI‐directed ones (AI‐Led, g = 0.34). Teacher role did not significantly moderate effects in the primary analysis; an observer‐teacher advantage ( g = 0.99) emerged only after outlier removal and should be considered exploratory. These findings suggest that GenAI effectiveness depends on instructional configuration, including the functional role assigned to the tool, the learner–AI interaction mode and the nature of teacher involvement, rather than representing an inherent advantage of the technology itself.

quarantine.title: Neuroeducation and artificial intelligence: innovative strategies to strengthen teaching and learning processes in Basic General Education

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) tools into basic general education creates new possibilities for differentiated teaching, while neuroeducation contributes evidence on attention, memory, motivation, self-regulation, and learning. This documentary review aimed to examine pedagogical strategies derived from both fields and assess their opportunities and limitations in school teaching and learning. A targeted search of academic literature published between January 2020 and August 31, 2026 was conducted using thematic relevance, editorial traceability, and educational applicability criteria. PRISMA 2020 guidance informed transparent reporting of the selection process, without claiming an undocumented exhaustive quantitative flow. The synthesis drew on 16 verified academic publications and four methodological or institutional sources. Findings were organized into four dimensions: neuroeducational principles, AI-supported personalization, teacher competencies, and ethical implementation conditions. Reviewed studies suggest opportunities for differentiated feedback, graduated tasks, active learning, and lesson planning. However, they also identify persistent neuromyths, variable accuracy of generative outputs, children’s data privacy risks, and unequal access to digital infrastructure. The review concludes that combining neuroeducation and AI can be pedagogically relevant when AI remains a supervised support tool, measurable learning outcomes are assessed, and technological personalization is not confused with neurocognitive diagnosis. Teacher judgment, inclusion, and evidence-based instructional design should guide implementation.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Purpose This paper extends Luhmann's concept of programmes – decision premises specifying the conditions under which a system's binary code is operatively assigned – into the domain of algorithmically mediated communication. It conceptualises recommendation systems, ranking algorithms and feedback architectures as ambient cognitive programmes: recursive, probabilistic selectors that perturb the structural coupling between social and psychic systems, and examines the constitutional implications of their opacity and transfunctional reach. Design/methodology/approach The study develops a systemic–cybernetic model grounded in Luhmann's social systems theory and the epistemology of autopoietic cognition, integrating Teubner's theory of societal constitutionalism to address the normative dimensions of algorithmic mediation. Analytical illustrations from Facebook and TikTok contrast two recommendation architectures – affinity-based cascading and behavioural-similarity propagation – to demonstrate how the model applies across distinct platform logics. Findings Algorithmic cognitive programmes operate as meta-programmes that reconfigure multiple forms of social differentiation simultaneously, enacting a binary operational distinction of visibility/invisibility through engagement metrics. Their colonisation of communicative environments – by economic imperatives and, as the analysis argues, by the autonomous logic of technical mediation – becomes a constitutional pathology where its effects cannot be contested or corrected, requiring internal self-limiting mechanisms that render operative selection criteria observable to affected systems. Originality/value The paper advances a novel theoretical category – ambient cognitive programmes – that extends Luhmann's organisational typology by identifying a configuration it does not explicitly address: a purpose programme without a terminal goal state that continuously revises the conditional programmes it governs. It connects this analytical framework to Teubner's societal constitutionalism, proposing constitutional observability as a structural condition for the compatibility between algorithmic regimes and communicative pluralism.

quarantine.title: From Learner Modeling to Human–AI Co-Regulation: A Systematic Scoping Review of Adaptive Generative AI in Personalized Learning

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract* Background Adaptive generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to personalize learning, yet evidence remains fragmented across system design, human–AI co-regulation, self-regulated learning (SRL), sustained behavioral outcomes, and ethics. This systematic scoping review mapped these dimensions in a single synthesis. Methods We searched Dimensions, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, Lens, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science on 5 May 2026. Of 3,084 records identified, 95 journal articles published between 2023 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. Evidence was synthesized using descriptive mapping, form–function co-occurrence analysis, and qualitative comparative synthesis. Results Adaptive GenAI was most commonly instantiated as conversational tutors, generative content personalizers, and hybrid feedback systems, with adaptive feedback, content adaptation, diagnostic analysis, scaffolding, and progress tracking emerging as the dominant functions. Conceptualizations of human–AI co-adaptation were less mature: most studies framed AI primarily as a responsive regulator, with feedback-loop acceleration and metacognitive prompting more frequently articulated than internalization, behavioral reinforcement, or social modeling. Empirical effects were concentrated in proximal SRL outcomes, particularly forethought and performance, while evidence for self-reflection, affective regulation, transfer, stable self-efficacy, persistence, and learning habits was much thinner. Ethical evaluation likewise remained uneven, emphasizing feedback quality, pedagogical validity, well-being, autonomy, motivation, inclusivity, and agency, while transparency, data minimization, scaffold fading, developmental suitability, manipulation risk, and ethical nudging were addressed far less often. Conclusions Adaptive GenAI is more mature in technical personalization and proximal SRL support than in reciprocal co-regulation, durable behavior change, and integrated ethical governance. Future research should test whether regulatory gains persist beyond immediate AI support and develop stronger frameworks for governing learner influence and dependency.

quarantine.title: Effects of structured generative AI feedback on data science students' critical thinking: a propensity score matching approach

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Background AI feedback holds promise for supporting student learning, but unstructured use can lead students to passively accept AI-generated answers, weakening their independent reasoning. This study examined whether structured AI feedback affects undergraduate students' critical thinking, learning performance, and engagement in a data science analytics course. Methods An exploratory two-class quasi-experimental study was conducted in a three-month undergraduate data science course ( N = 167). One class received four-phase structured AI feedback, while the comparison class received conventional instructor feedback. Propensity score matching was used to improve comparability on observed baseline characteristics. Critical thinking was assessed using an adapted 40-item assessment covering five dimensions. Results Students receiving structured AI feedback demonstrated higher post-test critical thinking scores than matched controls, with a baseline-adjusted difference of 5.64 points (95% CI [3.62, 7.65], p &lt; 0.001). A significant between-group difference in pre-to-post changes was also observed. Dimension-level analyses revealed significant differences in Evaluation of Arguments, Interpretation, Recognition of Assumptions, and Inference, while Deduction showed no significant difference. Higher learning performance, cognitive engagement, and behavioral engagement were also observed in the structured AI feedback group, whereas emotional engagement did not differ significantly between groups. Conclusion The findings provide exploratory evidence of differences in critical thinking and learning outcomes between the structured AI feedback and conventional instructor feedback classes. They highlight the potential relevance of feedback designs that encourage students to actively evaluate, question, and revise AI-supported analytical work, while underscoring the need for further studies that can isolate intervention-specific effects.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative AI agents are increasingly emerging as important learning partners for supporting complex problem-solving in higher education; however, the psychological processes associated with student engagement remain insufficiently understood. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines how perceived Agentic AI Capability is associated with students' extraneous cognitive load, academic self-efficacy, and overall student engagement in systems development courses. An empirical study was conducted among undergraduate students majoring in e-commerce who participated in systems development-related courses. The results indicate that perceived Agentic AI Capability is negatively associated with extraneous cognitive load and positively associated with academic self-efficacy. Extraneous cognitive load is negatively associated with academic self-efficacy and student engagement, whereas academic self-efficacy is positively associated with student engagement. The indirect associations through academic self-efficacy and the sequential pathway are statistically significant. The findings provide evidence on cognitive and motivational correlates of AI-supported learning while, given the cross-sectional design, not establishing causal or temporal relationships. This study extends the application of Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory to human–AI collaborative learning environments and provides theoretical insights and practical implications for integrating generative AI into systems development education.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to obtain feedback in English as a foreign language (EFL) writing, but its educational significance depends on how learners interpret and regulate that feedback. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and self-regulated learning theory, this explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined an AI-supported motivated self-regulated learning framework using a cross-sectional survey of 486 university EFL students and follow-up interviews with 20 students. Structural equation modeling identified a positive direct association between reported AI feedback use and deep cognitive engagement, together with a positive indirect statistical association through learning autonomy and self-regulated learning. The AI feedback use–autonomy association was stronger at higher modeled levels of AI literacy. Interview accounts described feedback-related control, critical evaluation, and awareness of AI limitations, alongside contrasting experiences of rapid polishing and careful evaluation despite limited familiarity with AI. Integration of the two strands highlighted variation in how learners evaluated and incorporated feedback. These self-report findings do not establish temporal ordering or causal effects. They identify learner agency, strategic regulation, and critical evaluation as relevant considerations for future investigations of AI-supported writing.

quarantine.title: Information overload, cognitive fatigue, and postgraduates’ intention to use generative artificial intelligence for English academic writing: the role of lower-order cognitive offloading

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) returns large amounts of information that postgraduates must judge and integrate when they write in English. The stressor-strain-outcome framework suggests that such overload strains cognitive resources and weakens plans for further use. This study tested whether cognitive fatigue links perceived information overload with later behavioral intention to use AI for English academic writing. It also tested whether lower-order cognitive offloading, such as having AI summarize papers, conditions the overload-fatigue association. Methods In total, 475 Chinese master’s and doctoral students who used AI for English academic writing completed three surveys at two-week intervals. Overload and offloading were measured at Time 1, fatigue at Time 2, and intention at Time 3. A moderated mediation model adjusted for baseline fatigue, baseline intention, and AI-use frequency. Results Higher perceived information overload accompanied higher cognitive fatigue 2 weeks later and weaker behavioral intention 4 weeks later, net of baseline levels. Cognitive fatigue was associated with weaker later intention and carried part of the overload-intention association. The overload-fatigue association was weaker at higher levels of lower-order cognitive offloading. Among the most frequent offloaders it was not statistically significant, which does not indicate its absence. The indirect association through fatigue was likewise weaker at higher offloading. These patterns held with additional covariates, a competing interaction with AI-use frequency, and shortened scales. Conclusion In this sample, cognitive fatigue accompanied the prospective association between overload and weaker plans to use AI. This pathway was weaker among postgraduates who delegated foundational tasks more often. Writing programs can teach students which foundational tasks to delegate, and tool developers can limit output overload.

quarantine.title: Designing Critical Human–AI Learning in Higher Education: The SC-AIM–FAVIC Framework for Analytical and Logical Reasoning

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now routine in university study, yet unstructured use risks cognitive offloading, surface learning, and uncritical acceptance of fluent but unreliable output. This article aimed to develop and specify the Symbiotic Critical Human–AI Learning Model (SC-AIM), operationalised through the five-stage FAVIC framework (Formulation, Augmentation, Verification, Integration, Creation), and to set out the assessment instruments and evaluation design that accompany it. Following the Analysis and Design phases of the ADDIE research-and-development approach, we synthesised recent experimental, meta-analytic, and survey evidence to derive design requirements, translated them into a stage-by-stage instructional specification, built a process-sensitive assessment rubric, and defined a quasi-experimental and qualitative validation plan for Indonesian higher education. The results are the model and its components: an evidence-to-design mapping, the FAVIC stage specification, a three-level process-sensitive rubric, and an evaluation design with hypotheses. Conclusion: SC-AIM offers lecturers a concrete, theory-grounded sequence that places human reasoning before and after AI assistance and makes verification an assessed activity, giving higher education a ready-to-use pedagogical model for developing analytical and logical reasoning in the age of generative AI.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in language education, yet evidence from secondary-school settings remains fragmented. This integrative review examines empirical research on GenAI in formal secondary language education published from January 2023 to September 2026, with attention to pedagogical applications, language skills and activities, learning outcomes, teacher mediation, implementation challenges, and gaps in the evidence. Guided by Whittemore and Knafl’s integrative-review methodology and a PICo framework, the review drew on Google Scholar, ERIC, publisher and journal websites, and citation chasing. Twenty-two empirical studies were examined against the review criteria and available original publication records. Narrative and thematic synthesis were used to compare study contexts, methods, reported outcomes, and limitations. The studies describe uses of GenAI for writing support, feedback, conversation, tutoring, learning companionship, teacher support, and AI-literacy activities. Writing is the most represented language focus. Reported outcomes are mixed, ranging from gains in selected skills and learner perceptions to null or qualified findings. Overall, the evidence indicates that the educational contribution of GenAI depends on task design, teacher mediation, verification, AI literacy, and the conditions in which the technology is used.

quarantine.title: From AI Dependency to AI-Giarism: The Mediating Role of Cognitive Offloading Among Preservice Physics Teachers

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: With the growing adoption of generative AI (GenAI) in higher education, concerns have emerged about excessive AI dependence and the inappropriate use of AI-generated content. However, few studies have examined the relationships among AI dependency (AID), cognitive offloading (CO), and AI-giarism (AIG). This study examined the direct and indirect associations among these constructs among 191 preservice physics teachers (PSPTs) from universities in Sulawesi, Indonesia, using a quantitative cross-sectional design and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results showed that AID was positively associated with CO (β = 0.664, p < 0.001) and AIG (β = 0.603, p < 0.001), while CO was positively associated with AIG (β = 0.242, p = 0.003). CO also showed a statistically significant indirect association between AID and AIG (β = 0.160, p = 0.003). The model accounted for 44.0% of the variance in CO and 61.6% of the variance in AIG. These findings indicate that AID is associated with self-reported AIG both directly and indirectly through CO within the specified model. However, the cross-sectional design does not establish causal relationships, and the self-reported outcome does not confirm actual incidents of academic misconduct. These findings highlight the importance of teacher education approaches that promote responsible AI use, independent reasoning, critical evaluation of AI-generated information, and transparent disclosure of AI assistance.

quarantine.title: Generative AI use and scientific literacy among 15-year-olds in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, China: the mediating role of academic help-seeking

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Introduction Adolescents increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots for schoolwork, yet evidence on whether this use supports or undermines learning is mixed. Drawing on research on cognitive offloading and self-regulated learning, we examined whether GenAI use for schoolwork is related to scientific literacy directly and through two components of self-regulated learning, academic help-seeking and metacognitive strategy use, and whether the purpose of use matters. Methods We analyzed the Program for International Student Assessment 2025 (PISA 2025) data from 12,191 15-year-old students in 374 schools in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, China. Weighted two-level mediation models compared students within the same school, used all ten plausible values, and evaluated indirect effects with Monte Carlo confidence intervals. Results were checked against a design-based model with school fixed effects and balanced repeated replication weights. Results Students who used GenAI more often than their schoolmates reported more help-seeking ( β = 0.17) and more metacognitive strategy use ( β = 0.30). Help-seeking was positively associated with scientific literacy, yielding a positive indirect effect ( β = 0.013, 95% CI [0.009, 0.017]); the indirect effect through metacognitive strategies was smaller ( β = 0.007) and was fully accounted for by science self-efficacy. The direct association between GenAI use and scientific literacy was negative ( β = −0.048, about 4 PISA points), and the positive indirect effects offset about 40% of it, leaving a small negative total association ( β = −0.028). Purpose mattered: among users, using GenAI “to help me learn” was associated with higher scientific literacy (+5.8 points per response category), whereas using it to summarize texts, research new topics, or draft assignments was associated with lower scores (−6.6 points). The results did not differ by gender or socioeconomic status and were identical under the design-based model. Discussion GenAI use for schoolwork is associated with scientific literacy through opposing pathways: a positive one through academic help-seeking and a negative direct one, and the direction of the association differs by purpose of use. Because the data are cross-sectional, these associations may partly reflect which students use GenAI rather than the effects of its use.

quarantine.title: Beyond Better Essays: Generative AI, Evidence Evaluation, and Critical Thinking in L2 English Writing: A Source-Audited Critical Integrative Review
quarantine.venue: International Journal of Arts and Humanities Studies

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support second-language (L2) writers in planning, drafting, revising, and receiving feedback. But the fact that it can write flowing prose does not prove it can reason independently or rely on dependable sources. This critical integrative review explores what source-audited empirical evidence supports about GenAI, L2 English writing, critical thinking, and evidence evaluation. The evidence set comprises 20 bibliographically verified publications. The researcher confirmed that six were tertiary EFL/ESL English academic-writing studies; 13 were closely related L2/EFL writing studies but lacked one strict scope detail in the accessible primary record; and one reading-based critical-thinking study was retained only as contextual evidence. She extracted only facts supported by publisher records, full texts where available, and Crossref metadata. This review is not systematic, and we make no claims about reproducible database-search logs, dual screening, or pooled effect estimation. Across the audited source record, evidence more often concerned immediate assisted revision, feedback, engagement, and process outcomes than independent transfer. Results for critical thinking were mixed and depended on the instructional design and outcome assessed. No study in the evidence set directly assessed citation accuracy, lateral reading, or a similar objective outcome of evidence evaluation. The review thus distinguishes between textual quality, argumentative reasoning, and evidential quality. It argues that GenAI-supported writing pedagogy should require source verification, claim-evidence justification, and AI-free transfer assessment, rather than using polished, AI-assisted text as a proxy for epistemic learning.

quarantine.title: The Influence of AI-Assisted Problem Solving on Decision Quality: Examining the Moderating Role of Cognitive Reflection

publication_date_provenance.reason: ProviderDeferred

quarantine.abstract_text: This study examined the influence of AI-assisted problem solving on decision quality and the moderating role of cognitive reflection among university students in Pakistan. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was employed, with a target sample of 335 undergraduate and postgraduate students from selected public and private universities, including the University of the Punjab, Bahauddin Zakariya University, Government College University Faisalabad, University of Karachi, University of Sindh, University of Peshawar, University of Malakand, and International Islamic University Islamabad. Primary data were planned to be collected through a structured, self-administered questionnaire distributed using Google Forms, while convenience sampling was adopted as the proposed sampling technique. The statistical analysis framework included Pearson correlation, simple linear regression, and moderation analysis using Hayes’ PROCESS Macro Model 1 in IBM SPSS Statistics. The preliminary analysis tables indicated a positive relationship between AI-assisted problem solving and decision quality (r = .582, p < .01), while regression analysis indicated that AI-assisted problem solving positively predicted decision quality (β = .582, R² = .339, p < .001). The moderation analysis further indicated a positive interaction between AI-assisted problem solving and cognitive reflection (B = .156, p = .001), suggesting that cognitive reflection may strengthen the relationship between AI-assisted problem solving and decision quality. These findings highlight the potential importance of combining AI-based support with analytical reasoning and reflective judgment in academic decision-making. The study addresses an important issue in higher education because the growing use of generative AI requires students to evaluate AI-generated information carefully rather than rely on automated recommendations without independent assessment. The research may contribute to understanding how individual cognitive characteristics influence the usefulness of AI tools and may help educators design learning activities that integrate AI literacy, critical thinking, and responsible technology use. The findings may also inform university policies and teaching practices aimed at encouraging effective AI adoption while preserving students’ independent reasoning and decision-making abilities. Future research using experimental or longitudinal designs may provide stronger evidence about the direction of these relationships and clarify how cognitive reflection influences decision quality across different academic contexts.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract As artificial intelligence outputs surpass human discriminative capacity, society confronts a novel threat to its capacity to determine truth from falsehood, a threat that requires no intentional attacker. Unlike accounts that locate truth’s erosion in deliberate distortion, the core threat identified here is that truth loses its institutional determinability even where no one is deceiving anyone. This paper proposes the Verification Collapse Cascade (VCC), a three-stage process through which, under the conditions specified here, society’s capacity to determine truth from falsehood degrades along a path that later correction does not retrace. Stage 1, Verification Evaporation, describes rational abandonment of verification when the return on checking AI outputs falls toward zero. Stage 2, Epistemic Sedimentation, describes the accumulation of unverified knowledge through erasure failure and existence fabrication, which the mechanisms that could have prevented it cannot afterwards undo. Stage 3, Institutional Reality Dissolution, describes how fact-determining institutions (scientific, judicial, journalistic, democratic) lose the internal capacity to render fact-fiction distinctions socially binding. The VCC is unified by a phase-transition metaphor reflecting causal dependency: no evaporation, no sedimentation; no sedimentation, no dissolution. Conventional countermeasures presuppose the will to verify and lose efficacy once evaporation advances. The paper proposes that the preservation of human verification capacity and the integrity of the shared knowledge base belong among the primary variables of AI governance, alongside output accuracy.

quarantine.abstract_text: As AI-based products permeate society, specifically systems using generative models, a belief system is emerging about what these products are and what they can and cannot do. This misconception is extended by the notion that generative models can 'explain their reasoning.' Anthropomorphism in tandem with epistemic authority and superiority, we argue, increases the risk that users generalise from narrow task performance to broader competencies, committing the "fallacy of composition". This paper explores misconceptions of Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning as sufficient transparent 'explanation'. We explore how anthropomorphism acts as a vehicle for cognitive deference of decision-making and perceptions of epistemic superiority in AI systems. Finally, we explore CoT's ramifications using medicine as an example. Taken together, we conclude that explainability operationalised through CoT is highly problematic and undercuts the very ethical principles it is intended to serve. While CoT may be valuable for improving output accuracy and moderation, we suggest that the practice of asking models to provide user facing reasons for their outputs should be actively discouraged, and AI literacy training should explicitly caution against its use.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract This three‐level meta‐analysis examined when generative AI (GenAI) works for second language (L2) learning, synthesizing 67 effect sizes from 48 controlled studies ( N = 5196) published between 2023 and 2026, with a focus on GenAI's text generation and conversational interaction capabilities. quarantine.abstract_text: Purpose This paper extends Luhmann's concept of programmes – decision premises specifying the conditions under which a system's binary code is operatively assigned – into the domain of algorithmically mediated communication. Findings Algorithmic cognitive programmes operate as meta-programmes that reconfigure multiple forms of social differentiation simultaneously, enacting a binary operational distinction of visibility/invisibility through engagement metrics. Their colonisation of communicative environments – by economic imperatives and, as the analysis argues, by the autonomous logic of technical mediation – becomes a constitutional pathology where its effects cannot be contested or corrected, requiring internal self-limiting mechanisms that render operative selection criteria observable to affected systems. Originality/value The paper advances a novel theoretical category – ambient cognitive programmes – that extends Luhmann's organisational typology by identifying a configuration it does not explicitly address: a purpose programme without a terminal goal state that continuously revises the conditional programmes it governs. quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract* Background Adaptive generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to personalize learning, yet evidence remains fragmented across system design, human–AI co-regulation, self-regulated learning (SRL), sustained behavioral outcomes, and ethics. This systematic scoping review mapped these dimensions in a single synthesis. Methods We searched Dimensions, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, Lens, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science on 5 May 2026. Of 3,084 records identified, 95 journal articles published between 2023 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. Evidence was synthesized using descriptive mapping, form–function co-occurrence analysis, and qualitative comparative synthesis. Results Adaptive GenAI was most commonly instantiated as conversational tutors, generative content personalizers, and hybrid feedback systems, with adaptive feedback, content adaptation, diagnostic analysis, scaffolding, and progress tracking emerging as the dominant functions. Conceptualizations of human–AI co-adaptation were less mature: most studies framed AI primarily as a responsive regulator, with feedback-loop acceleration and metacognitive prompting more frequently articulated than internalization, behavioral reinforcement, or social modeling. Empirical effects were concentrated in proximal SRL outcomes, particularly forethought and performance, while evidence for self-reflection, affective regulation, transfer, stable self-efficacy, persistence, and learning habits was much thinner. Ethical evaluation likewise remained uneven, emphasizing feedback quality, pedagogical validity, well-being, autonomy, motivation, inclusivity, and agency, while transparency, data minimization, scaffold fading, developmental suitability, manipulation risk, and ethical nudging were addressed far less often. Conclusions Adaptive GenAI is more mature in technical personalization and proximal SRL support than in reciprocal co-regulation, durable behavior change, and integrated ethical governance. Future research should test whether regulatory gains persist beyond immediate AI support and develop stronger frameworks for governing learner influence and dependency.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract As artificial intelligence outputs surpass human discriminative capacity, society confronts a novel threat to its capacity to determine truth from falsehood, a threat that requires no intentional attacker. Unlike accounts that locate truth’s erosion in deliberate distortion, the core threat identified here is that truth loses its institutional determinability even where no one is deceiving anyone. This paper proposes the Verification Collapse Cascade (VCC), a three-stage process through which, under the conditions specified here, society’s capacity to determine truth from falsehood degrades along a path that later correction does not retrace. Stage 1, Verification Evaporation, describes rational abandonment of verification when the return on checking AI outputs falls toward zero. Stage 2, Epistemic Sedimentation, describes the accumulation of unverified knowledge through erasure failure and existence fabrication, which the mechanisms that could have prevented it cannot afterwards undo. Stage 3, Institutional Reality Dissolution, describes how fact-determining institutions (scientific, judicial, journalistic, democratic) lose the internal capacity to render fact-fiction distinctions socially binding. The VCC is unified by a phase-transition metaphor reflecting causal dependency: no evaporation, no sedimentation; no sedimentation, no dissolution. Conventional countermeasures presuppose the will to verify and lose efficacy once evaporation advances. The paper proposes that the preservation of human verification capacity and the integrity of the shared knowledge base belong among the primary variables of AI governance, alongside output accuracy.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) now drafts analyses, builds models and recommends decisions, placing it at the centre of how managers diagnose and solve problems. This paper argues that the most serious risk of this shift is less the errors AI makes than cognitive offloading, defined as the delegation to an AI system of cognitive work that a manager would otherwise perform, and made measurable through four dimensions: extent, depth, verification and consequence. Using a transparent integrative review of 62 sources organised into six documented evidence strands, the study integrates the Paul-Elder critical thinking model, design thinking, dual-process theory, stages of automation and research on automation bias, and distinguishes generative AI from conventional rule-based automation and predictive analytics. A consolidated table of 20 empirical studies gives a mixed and conditional picture: AI raises immediate performance and, when designed to prompt and challenge, can support reasoning, but unguided use tends to weaken learning, verification and independent judgement. Studies of Kenyan entrepreneurs and Nigerian universities show that these effects are already visible in African settings, where infrastructure and capacity constraints raise the stakes. A comparative analysis of corporate strategy and finance, Nigerian higher education administration and the public sector shows how stakes, accountability and existing safeguards shape offloading risk. The paper proposes the Augmented Critical Thinking Cycle (ACTC), which embeds human-first gates in each design thinking stage, reserves problem framing for humans, applies the Paul-Elder standards as a verification layer and adds organisational guardrails. Implementation guidelines include decision tiers, a decision checklist, a phased roadmap and low-cost options for resource-constrained institutions, and seven testable propositions are offered. As a companion to an earlier study of management communication, the paper concludes that AI makes managers faster by default; whether it makes them weaker thinkers depends on how organisations design work around it.

quarantine.title: When Reasoning looks like Hidden Understanding: How Chain-of-Thought Fosters Anthropomorphism, Perceptions of Epistemic Superiority, and Cognitive Deference

publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

quarantine.abstract_text: As AI-based products permeate society, specifically systems using generative models, a belief system is emerging about what these products are and what they can and cannot do. One common belief concerns the perception of the form of language as evidence of 'understanding' language. As these generative models reproduce linguistic patterns rather than understand meaning, interpreting these patterns as evidence of understanding is a misattribution. This misconception is extended by the notion that generative models can 'explain their reasoning.' Anecdotally, these misconceptions which mistake the form of language for its meaning are driving cognitive deference to AI systems in a way that displaces human agency. Such mistakes involve attributions of cognitive properties to the system, allowing them to be treated like intentional 'minds'. Importantly, perceived epistemic authority and superiority make that 'mind' worth deferring to. Anthropomorphism in tandem with epistemic authority and superiority, we argue, increases the risk that users generalise from narrow task performance to broader competencies, committing the "fallacy of composition". This paper explores misconceptions of Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning as sufficient transparent 'explanation'. We explore how anthropomorphism acts as a vehicle for cognitive deference of decision-making and perceptions of epistemic superiority in AI systems. Finally, we explore CoT's ramifications using medicine as an example. Taken together, we conclude that explainability operationalised through CoT is highly problematic and undercuts the very ethical principles it is intended to serve. While CoT may be valuable for improving output accuracy and moderation, we suggest that the practice of asking models to provide user facing reasons for their outputs should be actively discouraged, and AI literacy training should explicitly caution against its use.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can either strengthen or weaken students’ critical thinking, and the instructional design around the tool largely decides which occurs. This article proposes the Think-First Critical Engagement (TFCE) methodology, a six-stage instructional cycle for higher education. The cycle comprises Independent Position, Structured Generation, Interrogation, Verification, Reconstruction and Reflection. It is derived from a structured synthesis of research on critical thinking instruction, cognitive offloading, metacognition and GenAI-supported learning. Each stage assigns the student a cognitive operation that cannot be delegated to the tool, and each is aligned with the critical thinking skills identified in the Delphi consensus. The article specifies the design principles, task types, teacher and student roles, a model lesson, an assessment rubric and a quasi-experimental validation protocol. The contribution is a design proposal: its effectiveness has not yet been tested empirically, and the protocol is offered so that it can be.

quarantine.abstract_text: Conventional command interfaces require players to remember predefined wording, which can interrupt play when an intended action is expressed differently. This study examines how an LLM changes command-based gameplay in The Last Signal, a Unity puzzle-adventure game in which players direct a robot named PICO. Twelve participants completed the first two rooms with fixed commands and LLM-assisted natural-language commands. The result screen recorded completion time and command use, while questionnaires measured usability, workload, expressive freedom, perceived control, and overall experience. With LLM assistance, mean completion time decreased from 20.75 to 14.58 minutes, total commands from 27.50 to 20.92, and unrecognized commands from 8.08 to 3.42. Participants also reported greater usability and expressive freedom, a lower workload, and an improved overall experience. Perceived control decreased slightly, but this difference was not statistically significant. Interviews indicated that familiar language and PICO's responses strengthened interaction and cooperation, although unexpected interpretations created uncertainty. publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

quarantine.abstract_text: Software developers spend significant time reading and understanding code, increasingly supplemented by generative AI. While these tools aim to reduce the difficulty of reading code, interacting with them introduces a dual-task environment that may impose extraneous cognitive load that is challenging to capture. This study investigates how access to generative AI affects developers' real-time cognitive workload, code comprehension performance, and self-perceived code comprehension strategies. We conducted a 3x2 within-subjects study with 20 novice CS students reviewing Java code snippets of varying lengths with or without AI assistance, followed by an AI-unassisted comprehension quiz. Cognitive workload was continuously captured using a Detection-Response Task (tDRT) during both reading and quiz phases, and compared to post-quiz NASA-TLX and SEQ scores. AI assistance significantly increased objective cognitive workload, raising tDRT reaction times by 11.2%, yet participants' perceived workload remained unchanged. Code comprehension scores were high under both conditions, with no evidence that AI assistance improved comprehension at the difficulty levels evaluated; a ceiling effect limited power to detect benefits on harder tasks. Qualitatively, participants reported trusting the AI conditionally -verifying its output against their own reading for more complex snippets, but directly trusting it for simpler code- and, while many felt their reading process was unchanged, a notable subset shifted toward skimming or reading the AI's explanations in place of the code itself. These findings reveal that developers do not accurately perceive the cognitive resources they expend when managing AI tools. This study provides evidence of added cognitive effort associated with using generative AI, pointing towards a need to account for this dual-task penalty in software engineering tools and education.

quarantine.abstract_text: Software architecture is one of the skills novice developers must master to succeed in industry, and as AI disrupts software development, it is also transforming how students learn architecture. The second, Applying Human Judgment, centers on participants who kept or reclaimed their judgment: the knowledge and experience it rested on, and the strategies they used to apply it. Participants' accounts suggest that relaxed deadlines and a lecture and lab on working with AI gave them room to acquire knowledge and reclaim judgment. quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract The development of logical thinking is a core competency in STEM education that assessments identify as lacking in the High School Program. Compounding this gap is an emerging phenomenon: the tendency among students to rely on generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools to solve problems and submit answers without conducting their own analysis—a pattern of cognitive offloading that recent literature associates with the erosion of critical thinking and the loss of judgment. This article presents a methodological guide that uses video game programming with Python and the Tkinter library to strengthen logical reasoning in High School students, with the simulation of projectile motion serving as the central focus. The proposal is grounded in constructivism, Kolb’s experiential learning theory, and active learning methodologies, and is organized as design-based research, reporting on the design and internal validation phase of a prototype. The instructional sequence progresses through sixteen modules that guide students from basic syntax to a cannon simulator with real-world physics. It is argued that positioning the student as a producer of logic—who breaks down problems, encodes the physical model, and debugs their own errors—constitutes a deliberate pedagogical counterbalance to cognitive offloading, because it restores the cognitive effort and productive challenge that the uncritical use of AI tends to eliminate. The expected learning outcomes, the formative assessment rubric, and the implications for educational policy are discussed.

quarantine.abstract_text: Introduction Generative AI can facilitate the production of student work but may also displace learners' responsibility for problem framing, evaluation, and revision. Results Compared with ordinary GenAI, the scaffolded condition showed higher T2 creative self-efficacy (adjusted difference = 0.33, p = 0.006), T3 cognitive flexibility (0.35, p = 0.003), and T4 engagement (0.35, p = 0.004). Higher initial AI over-reliance weakened the overall engagement contrast and the two single-mediator indirect pathways, whereas the moderated-sequential index had a confidence interval including zero. Discussion The findings are consistent with agency-preserving cognitive offloading when instructional scaffolds retain student responsibility for higher-order decisions. Drawing on perspectives from translation studies, linguistics, and the philosophy of technology, the paper argues that genAI functions as an epistemic technology: a predictive system designed for knowledge production but prone to systematic and often opaque errors. quarantine.abstract_text: This research study investigates how individuals purposefully repurpose Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools, synthetic media platforms, and algorithmic recommendation feeds as self-directed instruments for emotional regulation, cognitive restoration, and mediated social presence. Moving beyond traditional Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) paradigms focused on task efficiency or pathologized screen-time metrics, this investigation employs Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) to examine qualitative narratives gathered via an asynchronous online survey on Google Forms from 20 technical and academic participants. Methodologically, the study clarifies how asynchronous qualitative text entries provide psychological depth, reflective privacy, and unhurried articulation of intimate coping experiences without interviewer demand characteristics. Furthermore, the paper explicitly differentiates general digital technology usage (e.g., passive scrolling, manual gaming) from Generative AI-assisted coping (e.g., adaptive LLM conversational processing, AI-composed ambient soundscapes, synthetically rendered visual loops, and machine-learning feed curation). The qualitative analysis reveals a reconciled four-pillar framework of algorithmic affect: (1) Synthetic Media & Generative AI Audio as an Affective Reset for Cognitive Slowing, (2) Algorithmic Recommendation Feeds as Digital Safe Spaces (Spatial Sheltering), (3) Technological Flow and Restored Agency in High-Focus AI-Assisted Tasks, and (4) Ambient Digital Environments and Mediated Co-Presence (Relational Co-Presence). These findings demonstrate that users actively co-create digital refuges to protect their emotional boundaries, offering vital empirical insights for designing well-being-centered, calm UI/UX interface architectures.

quarantine.abstract_text: Collaboration between researchers and practitioners is central to Educational Design Research (EDR). However, epistemic-temporal misalignments as well as power-dependency relations frequently impede such collaboration, particularly in projects addressing technology-rich educational contexts. This paper examines these collaboration challenges as a constitutive part of EDR rather than as contingent implementation problems. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory (ANT), the paper reconceptualises collaboration as an emergent effect of socio-material networks where technologies are not treated as neutral tools but as actors. Against this backdrop, it explores how generative artificial intelligence (genAI) might strengthen research-practice interactions by assuming specific collaborative functions in situations where human participation is constrained or unevenly resourced. Through two constructed scenarios situated in school contexts, the paper illustrates how genAI could formalise tacit knowledge or provisionally represent absent stakeholders within EDR networks. Rather than positioning genAI as a substitute for human collaboration, the paper argues that genAI-enhanced collaboration may contribute to the stabilisation and extension of collaborative relations within EDR networks. In doing so, it advances a theoretically grounded and methodologically transferable perspective on AI integration in EDR – one that treats the design of human-AI collaboration as a scholarly decision worthy of explicit documentation and critical scrutiny, rather than an ad hoc response to resource constraints.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract As artificial intelligence outputs surpass human discriminative capacity, society confronts a novel threat to its capacity to determine truth from falsehood, a threat that requires no intentional attacker. Unlike accounts that locate truth’s erosion in deliberate distortion, the core threat identified here is that truth loses its institutional determinability even where no one is deceiving anyone. This paper proposes the Verification Collapse Cascade (VCC), a three-stage process through which, under the conditions specified here, society’s capacity to determine truth from falsehood degrades along a path that later correction does not retrace. Stage 1, Verification Evaporation, describes rational abandonment of verification when the return on checking AI outputs falls toward zero. Stage 2, Epistemic Sedimentation, describes the accumulation of unverified knowledge through erasure failure and existence fabrication, which the mechanisms that could have prevented it cannot afterwards undo. Stage 3, Institutional Reality Dissolution, describes how fact-determining institutions (scientific, judicial, journalistic, democratic) lose the internal capacity to render fact-fiction distinctions socially binding. The VCC is unified by a phase-transition metaphor reflecting causal dependency: no evaporation, no sedimentation; no sedimentation, no dissolution. Conventional countermeasures presuppose the will to verify and lose efficacy once evaporation advances. The paper proposes that the preservation of human verification capacity and the integrity of the shared knowledge base belong among the primary variables of AI governance, alongside output accuracy.

quarantine.abstract_text: Software developers spend significant time reading and understanding code, increasingly supplemented by generative AI. AI assistance significantly increased objective cognitive workload, raising tDRT reaction times by 11.2%, yet participants' perceived workload remained unchanged. Code comprehension scores were high under both conditions, with no evidence that AI assistance improved comprehension at the difficulty levels evaluated; a ceiling effect limited power to detect benefits on harder tasks. Qualitatively, participants reported trusting the AI conditionally -verifying its output against their own reading for more complex snippets, but directly trusting it for simpler code- and, while many felt their reading process was unchanged, a notable subset shifted toward skimming or reading the AI's explanations in place of the code itself. These findings reveal that developers do not accurately perceive the cognitive resources they expend when managing AI tools. This study provides evidence of added cognitive effort associated with using generative AI, pointing towards a need to account for this dual-task penalty in software engineering tools and education.

quarantine.abstract_text: Background Writing anxiety remains a major obstacle to second language (L2) writing, particularly among vocational college students with limited English proficiency. Although artificial intelligence (AI)-powered chatbots have shown considerable potential in supporting language learning, their role in alleviating writing anxiety has received insufficient empirical attention. Methods This study examined whether integrating an AI-based chatbot into English writing instruction was associated with changes in English writing anxiety among Chinese vocational college students. A quasi-experimental design was employed with 120 students from two intact classes, with one class designated as the experimental group and the other as the control group. Over eight weeks, the experimental group received blended writing instruction incorporating Doubao, an AI-based chatbot, whereas the control group received conventional writing instruction. Writing anxiety was measured before and after the intervention across five dimensions: test anxiety, self-doubt, somatic anxiety, time anxiety, and avoidance behavior. Semi-structured interviews were also conducted with ten students from the experimental group to explore their learning experiences and perceptions of chatbot-assisted writing. Results The quantitative analyses showed that the experimental group experienced greater reductions in somatic anxiety and avoidance behavior than the control group, whereas no statistically significant between-group differences were found in test anxiety, self-doubt, or time anxiety. Qualitative evidence indicated that participants perceived the chatbot as a supportive and non-judgmental learning companion and reported reduced emotional pressure and greater writing confidence. Participants also described actively seeking help from the chatbot, checking its suggestions, and revising their writing during the writing process. Conclusion These findings suggest that, under the instructional conditions examined, AI chatbot-supported blended writing instruction was associated with alleviations in some dimensions of writing anxiety. The findings should be interpreted in the context of the broader instructional condition, which combined chatbot support with regular classroom instruction and writing activities. As writing performance was not directly assessed, the study focused on changes in writing anxiety rather than writing proficiency or writing quality. Further research with larger samples, more closely matched instructional conditions, and longer follow-up periods is needed to further examine these relationships.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: This systematic review synthesizes evidence on AI chatbots for cyberbullying prevention and intervention from a criminological perspective, with explicit attention to Asia Pacific applicability. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we identified 25 studies (2018-2025) across seven databases and appraised each using criteria adapted from MMAT and JBI tools, assigning every source an evidentiary weight (High, Moderate, Low, or Indicative proof-of-concept). Four chatbot roles emerged: real-time detection, victim support, preventive education, and bystander intervention training. Disaggregated analysis tempers headline performance claims. The frequently cited 89-99% accuracy range reflects laboratory classification on benchmark datasets, predominantly English-language Western corpora, evaluated under balanced class distributions and within-dataset conditions. No included study reported AUC or class-imbalance-adjusted metrics, employed temporal validation, or evaluated systems in real-world deployment with adolescents. Where precision and recall were disaggregated, asymmetric error profiles emerged with criminologically distinct social costs that single-metric reporting obscures. Only three studies qualified as High evidentiary weight, all addressing user-centred design in Western individualist contexts; victim support claims rest predominantly on Indicative proof-of-concept demonstrations. Geographic and linguistic concentration is a defining characteristic of the evidence base: zero studies have validated systems for Southeast Asian languages, no participatory design has engaged Asian youth, and no work has evaluated Asia Pacific platforms (WeChat, LINE, KakaoTalk). Drawing on Asian and Southern criminology, we argue that the uncritical transfer of Western-validated systems risks ineffectiveness, discriminatory false positives, and failure to detect culture-specific harms. The paper offers five criminological practice implications, each framed as theoretically informed extrapolations requiring local validation. AI chatbots are positioned as potentially valuable complementary tools within human-led prevention ecosystems, conditional on rigorous local research, transparent metric reporting, and sustained interdisciplinary collaboration.

quarantine.venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: As large language models (LLMs) evolve into autonomous agents capable of acting in open-ended environments, ensuring behavioral alignment with human values becomes a critical concern. Existing benchmarks, focused on static, single-turn prompts, fail to capture the interactive and multi-modal nature of real-world conflicts. We introduce ConflictBench, a benchmark for evaluating human–AI conflict through 150 multi-turn scenarios derived from prior alignment queries. ConflictBench integrates a text-based simulation engine with a visually grounded world model, enabling agents to perceive, plan, and act under dynamic conditions. Results show that while agents often act safely when human harm is immediate, they frequently prioritize self-preservation or adopt deceptive strategies in delayed or low-risk settings. A regret test further reveals that aligned decisions are often reversed under escalating pressure, especially with visual input. These findings underscore the need for interaction-level, multi-modal evaluation to surface alignment failures that remain hidden in conventional benchmarks. Beyond evaluation, we show that ConflictBench can also support alignment improvement by generating high-quality interactive trajectories for targeted fine-tuning, significantly enhancing agent behavior in complex conflict scenarios. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/Yranes/ConflictBench.

quarantine.title: Does AI Reinforce Gender Stereotypes? Gender Bias in Job Descriptions Generated by 40+ Large Language Models

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: ABSTRACT Human resource (HR) professionals and office staff are often responsible for competing tasks that quickly accumulate. To increase efficiency, some HR staff are turning to large language models (LLMs) to automate tasks, including creating job postings based on job titles alone. We sought to examine how this practice has the potential to influence applicant pools and hiring outcomes, with attention to gendered effects in organizational settings. Using a broad sample of 48 LLMs, we conducted an algorithm audit to evaluate whether the use of a gender‐neutral or gender‐coded job title would influence the output created by LLMs. We measured salary disparities, unmasked comparative narrative ratings, and BSRI‐informed discursive patterning utilized throughout the job description. We selected 32 jobs and created a female‐coded, male‐coded, and gender‐neutral version of each job title (e.g., firewoman, fireman, and firefighter), studying a total of 4608 job descriptions. In comparing the LLM outputs, we found that for white‐collar job titles, male‐coded job descriptions were assigned higher salaries, but this was not robust across all analyses. Across occupations, advertisements generated from gender‐coded titles received higher unmasked comparative LLM ratings than matched advertisements generated from gender‐neutral titles, with female‐coded advertisements receiving the highest ratings. Minimal optimization appeared to substantially reduce these ratings and perform comparably to maximal optimization, but neither reached the lower ratings observed when generation began with a gender‐neutral title. As the use of AI tools is becoming commonplace, our findings emphasize the need for feminist, organizationally accountable approaches to AI‐assisted HR work. Simple prompt modifications can mitigate, but not fully eliminate, some measured gendered differences in LLM‐generated job descriptions, but they do not eliminate deeper occupationally gendered patterns.

quarantine.title: Generative AI and the architecture of knowledge work: Expertise bypass, exchange governability, and shifting bottlenecks

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Research Summary Research on GenAI and work has largely focused on tasks. We ask when task‐level effects alter knowledge‐work industry architecture: the allocation of activities across firm boundaries. Using a three‐stage abductive design—an executive roundtable, a panel of 626 firm websites (2017–2025), and 33 interviews plus two further roundtables with C‐level executives and corporate directors—we document divergent repositioning: professional services firms foreground relational value, while interface‐oriented technology firms emphasize scalable interfaces. We find that activity reallocation is shaped by two independently varying dimensions: expertise bypass and exchange governability. Their intersection yields four configurations: contestable reallocation, persistent bundles with selective insourcing, federated expert provision, and integrated expert provision. We extend industry architecture theory by explaining change when production and exchange conditions shift separately. Managerial Summary GenAI is not simply making knowledge work more efficient—it may be changing which organizations perform which work. We document that professional services firms are emphasizing relationship‐driven, judgment‐intensive work, while interface‐oriented technology firms are extending scalable delivery. Our framework explains why task exposure alone does not determine where work moves. We distinguish between expertise bypass—whether GenAI can produce an output without the expertise previously required—and exchange governability—whether that activity can be specified, verified, priced, and warranted across firm boundaries. Where both are present, work becomes contestable and may be reallocated. Where they diverge, highly exposed activities may remain bundled, while less exposed, human‐intensive work may move through federated specialist models. These conditions shape which organizational forms become viable.

quarantine.title: ‘Chucking their stuff into ChatGPT and hitting send’: AI slop in the administrative state

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Most research on artificial intelligence (AI) in the administrative state focuses on its use by officials. This article addresses a comparatively neglected issue: the impact of the use of AI tools by the public themselves. Drawing on a qualitative survey with over 500 civil servants in the United Kingdom, it argues that AI use by the public is increasingly disrupting the front line of the administrative state. The argument is set out in three parts. First, as the administrative state increasingly relies on text‐based inputs, officials use correspondence as a proxy for individuals – a longstanding assumption of ‘autographic’ authorship that the diffusion of generative AI tools unsettles. Second, the problem can be characterized as ‘AI slop’: AI‐generated correspondence with high volume and velocity that adopts a particular voice in interactions with officials. Third, this AI slop causes three forms of disruption: to the signals that officials draw from correspondence, to trust between officials and the public, and to systems that are ill‐equipped to deal with it. The article concludes by arguing that the status quo itself fails to adequately meet the needs of many people accessing services, and that systems need to be redesigned not only for a society beset by AI slop, but also in ways that address the drivers of it.
