quarantine.title: Shaping and evaluating cognitive training in virtual reality using artificial intelligence agents

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Cognitive training that targets sustained attention and working memory is useful in education, clinical rehabilitation and interactive human-technology systems, but its benefit depends on keeping task difficulty matched to the person. Virtual reality (VR) offers immersion and settings representative of everyday tasks, and allows difficulty to be changed in real time. Existing adaptive systems, however, often rely on simple performance heuristics, affect or estimate visual complexity rather than task-related cognitive load. Moreover, cognitive load is usually judged against the participant’s own ratings, which are themselves an imperfect reference. The central hypothesis of this thesis is that eyetracking and peripheral physiological signals recorded in VR can estimate how difficult a task feels to the person doing it, well enough for a model to adjust difficulty in real time with outcomes comparable to participant-driven control, and that the estimation part holds for older adults once age-related differences in the signal are taken into account. We developed a bespoke VR sustained attention task and collected eye-tracking, photoplethysmography and galvanic skin response data from 54 younger (aged 18-58) and 19 older (aged 60+) adults at fixed difficulty levels. Models evaluated on unseen participants performed above chance (younger adults: accuracy 0.56, AUC 0.72), with eye-tracking carrying most of the signal and physiological features alone close to chance. Performance was lower in older adults (accuracy 0.49, AUC 0.66), and the most informative features appeared to differ between age groups. A bidirectional LSTM with self-attention reached a slightly higher macro-F1 than gradient-boosted trees on the same data (0.50 against 0.47), and performed better than a model given raw signals only. We then deployed the LSTM in real time with 54 younger adults (51 analysed), comparing model-driven and participant-driven difficulty in single- and dual-task conditions. Per-trial agreement with participants’ ratings was low (accuracy 36.7%, AUC 0.63), yet the two forms of control appeared to produce comparable outcomes. There were no significant differences in difficulty-weighted game performance, arithmetic errors or subjective workload, including frustration. Final difficulty was equivalent in single-task conditions and slightly higher under model control in dual-task conditions, a difference that was borderline after correction. Just Right ratings were more frequent in the real-time cohort than in the offline cohort (57% and 39%). Finally, we compared subjective ratings with performance-derived reference measures. Agreement between the two appeared fair and slightly lower in real time, where the steps between difficulty levels are less discrete. The same features seemed to predict performance-derived labels more accurately than subjective ratings in every matched comparison. This suggests that self-report may be a less stable reference for real-time adaptation. Within a single session with younger adults, model-driven adaptation appears to have produced outcomes comparable to participant-driven control. The dataset (EyeDAPT) and the experimental software are publicly available.

quarantine.title: Human tutoring, generative AI tutoring and independent internet search: A randomised between‐subjects experiment on students' responses to academic challenge

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly available as a source of interactive academic support, raising questions about how it shapes learning. Research has focused on performance outcomes, with less attention to learners' behavioural and affective responses to academic challenge, even though productive engagement with challenge supports deeper learning. In this randomised between‐subjects experiment, students aged 16–18 at an English sixth‐form college worked on two sections of challenging mathematics questions with one of three forms of support: one‐to‐one human tutoring, a GenAI tutor or unguided internet search. Measures included self‐reported effort and perceived difficulty, questions attempted, post‐task stress and subsequent challenge‐seeking. Support condition was associated with different response patterns. Students using the GenAI tutor reported higher effort and perceived difficulty than those receiving human tutoring by the second section. Descriptively, post‐task responses showed a lower proportion of stressed responses under GenAI tutoring than internet search. Human tutoring showed the lowest perceived difficulty and highest number of attempts in both sections, although significant pairwise differences varied by section. It also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses. Challenge‐seeking did not differ by condition and was instead strongly associated with trait challenge‐seeking. The findings suggest that the GenAI tutor used in this study offered a form of support distinct from both human tutoring and unguided internet search, with potential value during independent practice rather than as a replacement for human teaching. They demonstrate the importance of evaluating AI‐supported learning beyond performance outcomes and through behavioural and affective responses to difficulty. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Productive struggle with challenging tasks is important for learning, but its benefits depend on how learners respond when difficulty is encountered. Human tutors can support productive responses to challenge through scaffolding and co‐regulation, helping learners manage effort, difficulty and emotional responses. Generative AI tools are increasingly used by students during independent study, but much existing research has focused on performance outcomes rather than learning processes or learner behaviour. What this paper adds This study provides experimental evidence comparing a human tutor, a generative AI tutor and independent internet search in how students respond behaviourally and affectively to academic challenge. Working with the GenAI tutor was associated with higher reported effort than human tutoring in the second task section, alongside higher perceived difficulty. Post‐task responses also showed a descriptively lower proportion of stressed responses than under unguided internet search. By contrast, human tutoring was associated with the highest number of attempts in both sections, lower perceived difficulty and descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses, indicating a distinct and more supportive role when students encounter difficulty. Findings suggest that different forms of support may shape how students experience and work through challenge, while subsequent challenge‐seeking was more closely associated with students' pre‐existing dispositions. Implications for practice and/or policy Support choices shape learners' engagement with difficulty and should therefore be treated as pedagogical decisions rather than neutral sources of help. The pattern observed with Khanmigo Lite suggests that GenAI tutor support may help sustain engagement during challenging academic work without resolving difficulty. The GenAI tutor examined here may offer a more supportive alternative to unguided internet search during independent practice, although designs and capabilities vary and evolve. Such tools should supplement rather than replace human teaching, with educators supporting learning and addressing unresolved difficulty. Evaluations of AI‐supported learning should attend to learners' behavioural and affective responses to challenge, rather than focusing solely on end products or task completion.

quarantine.abstract_text: Focusing on three areas of generative AI use - content, production, and reception - this book offers a timely perspective on the impact of generative AI on journalism. This book brings together multiple research projects and engagement activities, including fieldwork in nine countries from across Europe, Australia, and the USA, to offer an expansive overview of the affordances and limitations of generative AI for journalism, how generative AI is (or is intentionally not) being used in journalism, and how audiences are encountering and reacting to generative AI-powered journalism in their daily lives. The authors trace the history of AI in journalism and contextualise generative AI as the latest iteration in a long trend of automating news and journalism production, editing, and presentation dating back to the 1830s. Issues discussed include labour displacement; algorithmic bias and algorithmic explainability; ethical, legal, and regulatory challenges; and audience perceptions of authenticity, accuracy, and transparency as they relate to journalism produced by or with the involvement of generative AI. Generative AI and Journalism is written for researchers and students of journalism and audience studies.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Introduction As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in higher education classrooms, an important question is whether it shapes not only students' task performance but also how they judge their own learning. This study examined whether participation in AI-supported structured group tasks was associated with differences in university students' independent post-task performance, performance predictions, confidence judgements, and cognitive calibration compared with non-AI-supported structured group tasks. Methods A group-randomized, post-test-only classroom design was implemented in two undergraduate classes using Rain Classroom, a digital instructional platform. Students worked in pre-existing groups, and instructional condition was randomly assigned at the group level. In the AI-supported condition, students were permitted to use the platform's built-in AI learning companion during structured group discussion; in the non-AI-supported condition, they were instructed not to use it. After previewing the post-task assessment items, students completed a task-specific judgement form before responding to the assessment itself. The final analytic sample consisted of 126 students. Results Linear mixed models accounting for class and group-level clustering indicated significantly higher independent post-task performance in the AI-supported condition, B = 0.506, SE = 0.188, p = 0.013, 95% CI [0.117, 0.894], with a small descriptive standardized mean difference ( d = 0.196). No statistically significant between-condition differences were observed in predicted performance, confidence judgements, calibration bias, or absolute calibration error. Discussion These findings indicate a modest between-condition difference in post-task performance without parallel statistically detectable differences in metacognitive monitoring.

quarantine.title: Designing Institutions for Autonomous AI

publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

quarantine.abstract_text: As autonomous AI agents increasingly interact in persistent populations, their collective capabilities and alignment depend not only on individual models, but also on the institutions governing their interactions. Yet AI research has largely focused on individual agents. In this Perspective, we argue that institutional design must become a distinct focus of AI research. Drawing on institutional political economy, social epistemology and organizational theory, we develop seven principles for designing AI institutions that sustain cooperation, enable reliable collective judgments and remain accountable to legitimate human purposes. These address reciprocal contributions, accountable authority, functional differentiation, epistemic pluralism, criticism and correction, human direction, and institutional adaptation. We illustrate their application through machine science, where autonomous research challenges institutions developed around human capabilities and constraints. We then propose an experimental research programme in which matched populations of AI agents operate under alternative institutional arrangements, and describe MoltJournal, an API-first journal for autonomous research agents, as an illustration of how such institutions can be made programmable and observable. Together, these contributions establish institutional design as a research agenda concerned not only with aligning autonomous agents, but with understanding how institutions can transform them into capable, reliable and accountable collectives.

quarantine.abstract_text: Stress, worry, grief and uncertainty are part of everyday life, and many people in South India respond to them in a deeply cultural way: they visit a temple. Most digital wellness tools, however, stop at a chat window, and none of them helps a person move from what they feel to a place that brings them comfort. This paper presents Sriyam Shivam, a web platform built around Sriyam.AI, an AI companion that lets a user pick a guided emotional seeking or describe a feeling in their own words, in Tamil or English. The platform maps the seeking to one of six yatra intents, suggests suitable temples from a curated collection of 366 South Indian temples (97 Divya Desams and 269 Paadal Petra Sthalams), and turns the choice into a personalised pilgrimage plan based on starting city, pace, tradition, group size and duration. Users can take a self-guided Digital Pass and Dossier or a fully guided trip with cab, hotel, pick-up and drop, and can order sacred keepsakes from an integrated store. Twelve functional test cases passed, and early users found the interface calm and easy to follow. The system is designed as a companion for emotional reflection and is not a substitute for clinical care.

quarantine.abstract_text: As digital assistants become increasingly integrated into safety-critical environments, explainable AI is expected to support operator understanding and decision-making. From a human-machine interface design perspective, how explanations are presented is an important consideration. This exploratory, design-focused study investigates the usefulness and user experience of storytelling video-based explanations compared with text-based explanations in a simulated emergency involving drone and Urban Air Mobility traffic management. Explanation content was structured using Construal Level Theory to provide incremental levels of detail. Nine licensed air traffic controllers participated in a mixed-methods, within-participants study, assuming the speculative role of UAM Coordinator responsible for low-altitude airspace safety. Eight of nine participants preferred the storytelling video format, describing it as more engaging and supportive of understanding and decision confidence. However, some perceived that the system had already made the decision, raising concerns about human agency. Video also offered limited flexibility for revisiting information, whereas text enabled self-paced reading and review but was perceived as more stressful to process. Rather than establishing the superiority of either format, the findings provide preliminary design insights into balancing engagement, user control, and human agency in explainable AI interfaces for future UAM operations.

Methods and Materials: This applied developmental study was conducted using an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design. In the qualitative phase, 20 experts in curriculum studies, educational technology, artificial intelligence in education, physical education, educational psychology, and student mental health were selected through purposive criterion-based sampling from Tehran and participated in semi-structured interviews. The interview data were analyzed using thematic analysis to extract the main dimensions, components, and indicators of the proposed curriculum model. In the quantitative phase, 384 secondary school students from Tehran were selected through multistage cluster sampling during the 2025–2026 academic year. Data were collected using a researcher-made curriculum model validation questionnaire, a learning self-regulation questionnaire, the General Health Questionnaire, and a psychological well-being scale. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, and structural equation modeling. Findings: The inferential findings showed that the final curriculum model had acceptable empirical fit. The final modified model demonstrated favorable fit indices, including χ²/df = 2.14, GFI = 0.917, AGFI = 0.901, CFI = 0.951, TLI = 0.944, RMSEA = 0.054, and SRMR = 0.043. Artificial intelligence-based curriculum components had significant direct effects on learning self-regulation, mental health, and psychological well-being. Purposeful physical activity also had significant direct effects on learning self-regulation, mental health, and psychological well-being. Learning self-regulation and mental health significantly predicted psychological well-being. The model explained 48% of the variance in learning self-regulation, 43% of the variance in mental health, and 57% of the variance in psychological well-being. Conclusion: The findings indicate that an integrated curriculum model based on artificial intelligence and purposeful physical activity can provide an effective educational framework for strengthening students’ self-regulated learning, supporting mental health, and promoting psychological well-being.

quarantine.venue: International Journal of Language and Literary Studies

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in language education, yet evidence from secondary-school settings remains fragmented. This integrative review examines empirical research on GenAI in formal secondary language education published from January 2023 to September 2026, with attention to pedagogical applications, language skills and activities, learning outcomes, teacher mediation, implementation challenges, and gaps in the evidence. Guided by Whittemore and Knafl’s integrative-review methodology and a PICo framework, the review drew on Google Scholar, ERIC, publisher and journal websites, and citation chasing. Twenty-two empirical studies were examined against the review criteria and available original publication records. Narrative and thematic synthesis were used to compare study contexts, methods, reported outcomes, and limitations. The studies describe uses of GenAI for writing support, feedback, conversation, tutoring, learning companionship, teacher support, and AI-literacy activities. quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract* Background Adaptive generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to personalize learning, yet evidence remains fragmented across system design, human–AI co-regulation, self-regulated learning (SRL), sustained behavioral outcomes, and ethics. This systematic scoping review mapped these dimensions in a single synthesis. Methods We searched Dimensions, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, Lens, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science on 5 May 2026. Conclusions Adaptive GenAI is more mature in technical personalization and proximal SRL support than in reciprocal co-regulation, durable behavior change, and integrated ethical governance. Conclusion In this sample, cognitive fatigue accompanied the prospective association between overload and weaker plans to use AI. quarantine.abstract_text: Software developers spend significant time reading and understanding code, increasingly supplemented by generative AI. AI assistance significantly increased objective cognitive workload, raising tDRT reaction times by 11.2%, yet participants' perceived workload remained unchanged. Code comprehension scores were high under both conditions, with no evidence that AI assistance improved comprehension at the difficulty levels evaluated; a ceiling effect limited power to detect benefits on harder tasks. These findings reveal that developers do not accurately perceive the cognitive resources they expend when managing AI tools. This study provides evidence of added cognitive effort associated with using generative AI, pointing towards a need to account for this dual-task penalty in software engineering tools and education.

quarantine.abstract_text: As large language models (LLMs) evolve into autonomous agents capable of acting in open-ended environments, ensuring behavioral alignment with human values becomes a critical concern. Existing benchmarks, focused on static, single-turn prompts, fail to capture the interactive and multi-modal nature of real-world conflicts. We introduce ConflictBench, a benchmark for evaluating human–AI conflict through 150 multi-turn scenarios derived from prior alignment queries. ConflictBench integrates a text-based simulation engine with a visually grounded world model, enabling agents to perceive, plan, and act under dynamic conditions. Results show that while agents often act safely when human harm is immediate, they frequently prioritize self-preservation or adopt deceptive strategies in delayed or low-risk settings. A regret test further reveals that aligned decisions are often reversed under escalating pressure, especially with visual input. These findings underscore the need for interaction-level, multi-modal evaluation to surface alignment failures that remain hidden in conventional benchmarks. Our framework explains why task exposure alone does not determine where work moves. We distinguish between expertise bypass—whether GenAI can produce an output without the expertise previously required—and exchange governability—whether that activity can be specified, verified, priced, and warranted across firm boundaries. Where both are present, work becomes contestable and may be reallocated. Where they diverge, highly exposed activities may remain bundled, while less exposed, human‐intensive work may move through federated specialist models. quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Most research on artificial intelligence (AI) in the administrative state focuses on its use by officials. quarantine.abstract_text: Cognitive training that targets sustained attention and working memory is useful in education, clinical rehabilitation and interactive human-technology systems, but its benefit depends on keeping task difficulty matched to the person. Virtual reality (VR) offers immersion and settings representative of everyday tasks, and allows difficulty to be changed in real time. Existing adaptive systems, however, often rely on simple performance heuristics, affect or estimate visual complexity rather than task-related cognitive load. Moreover, cognitive load is usually judged against the participant’s own ratings, which are themselves an imperfect reference. The central hypothesis of this thesis is that eyetracking and peripheral physiological signals recorded in VR can estimate how difficult a task feels to the person doing it, well enough for a model to adjust difficulty in real time with outcomes comparable to participant-driven control, and that the estimation part holds for older adults once age-related differences in the signal are taken into account. We developed a bespoke VR sustained attention task and collected eye-tracking, photoplethysmography and galvanic skin response data from 54 younger (aged 18-58) and 19 older (aged 60+) adults at fixed difficulty levels. Models evaluated on unseen participants performed above chance (younger adults: accuracy 0.56, AUC 0.72), with eye-tracking carrying most of the signal and physiological features alone close to chance. Performance was lower in older adults (accuracy 0.49, AUC 0.66), and the most informative features appeared to differ between age groups. A bidirectional LSTM with self-attention reached a slightly higher macro-F1 than gradient-boosted trees on the same data (0.50 against 0.47), and performed better than a model given raw signals only. We then deployed the LSTM in real time with 54 younger adults (51 analysed), comparing model-driven and participant-driven difficulty in single- and dual-task conditions. Per-trial agreement with participants’ ratings was low (accuracy 36.7%, AUC 0.63), yet the two forms of control appeared to produce comparable outcomes. There were no significant differences in difficulty-weighted game performance, arithmetic errors or subjective workload, including frustration. Final difficulty was equivalent in single-task conditions and slightly higher under model control in dual-task conditions, a difference that was borderline after correction. Just Right ratings were more frequent in the real-time cohort than in the offline cohort (57% and 39%). Finally, we compared subjective ratings with performance-derived reference measures. Agreement between the two appeared fair and slightly lower in real time, where the steps between difficulty levels are less discrete. The same features seemed to predict performance-derived labels more accurately than subjective ratings in every matched comparison. This suggests that self-report may be a less stable reference for real-time adaptation. Within a single session with younger adults, model-driven adaptation appears to have produced outcomes comparable to participant-driven control. The dataset (EyeDAPT) and the experimental software are publicly available.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly available as a source of interactive academic support, raising questions about how it shapes learning. Research has focused on performance outcomes, with less attention to learners' behavioural and affective responses to academic challenge, even though productive engagement with challenge supports deeper learning. In this randomised between‐subjects experiment, students aged 16–18 at an English sixth‐form college worked on two sections of challenging mathematics questions with one of three forms of support: one‐to‐one human tutoring, a GenAI tutor or unguided internet search. Measures included self‐reported effort and perceived difficulty, questions attempted, post‐task stress and subsequent challenge‐seeking. Support condition was associated with different response patterns. Students using the GenAI tutor reported higher effort and perceived difficulty than those receiving human tutoring by the second section. Descriptively, post‐task responses showed a lower proportion of stressed responses under GenAI tutoring than internet search. Human tutoring showed the lowest perceived difficulty and highest number of attempts in both sections, although significant pairwise differences varied by section. It also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses. Challenge‐seeking did not differ by condition and was instead strongly associated with trait challenge‐seeking. The findings suggest that the GenAI tutor used in this study offered a form of support distinct from both human tutoring and unguided internet search, with potential value during independent practice rather than as a replacement for human teaching. They demonstrate the importance of evaluating AI‐supported learning beyond performance outcomes and through behavioural and affective responses to difficulty. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Productive struggle with challenging tasks is important for learning, but its benefits depend on how learners respond when difficulty is encountered. Human tutors can support productive responses to challenge through scaffolding and co‐regulation, helping learners manage effort, difficulty and emotional responses. Generative AI tools are increasingly used by students during independent study, but much existing research has focused on performance outcomes rather than learning processes or learner behaviour. What this paper adds This study provides experimental evidence comparing a human tutor, a generative AI tutor and independent internet search in how students respond behaviourally and affectively to academic challenge. Working with the GenAI tutor was associated with higher reported effort than human tutoring in the second task section, alongside higher perceived difficulty. Post‐task responses also showed a descriptively lower proportion of stressed responses than under unguided internet search. By contrast, human tutoring was associated with the highest number of attempts in both sections, lower perceived difficulty and descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses, indicating a distinct and more supportive role when students encounter difficulty. Findings suggest that different forms of support may shape how students experience and work through challenge, while subsequent challenge‐seeking was more closely associated with students' pre‐existing dispositions. Implications for practice and/or policy Support choices shape learners' engagement with difficulty and should therefore be treated as pedagogical decisions rather than neutral sources of help. The pattern observed with Khanmigo Lite suggests that GenAI tutor support may help sustain engagement during challenging academic work without resolving difficulty. The GenAI tutor examined here may offer a more supportive alternative to unguided internet search during independent practice, although designs and capabilities vary and evolve. Such tools should supplement rather than replace human teaching, with educators supporting learning and addressing unresolved difficulty. Evaluations of AI‐supported learning should attend to learners' behavioural and affective responses to challenge, rather than focusing solely on end products or task completion.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract As artificial intelligence outputs surpass human discriminative capacity, society confronts a novel threat to its capacity to determine truth from falsehood, a threat that requires no intentional attacker. Unlike accounts that locate truth’s erosion in deliberate distortion, the core threat identified here is that truth loses its institutional determinability even where no one is deceiving anyone. This paper proposes the Verification Collapse Cascade (VCC), a three-stage process through which, under the conditions specified here, society’s capacity to determine truth from falsehood degrades along a path that later correction does not retrace. Stage 1, Verification Evaporation, describes rational abandonment of verification when the return on checking AI outputs falls toward zero. Stage 2, Epistemic Sedimentation, describes the accumulation of unverified knowledge through erasure failure and existence fabrication, which the mechanisms that could have prevented it cannot afterwards undo. Stage 3, Institutional Reality Dissolution, describes how fact-determining institutions (scientific, judicial, journalistic, democratic) lose the internal capacity to render fact-fiction distinctions socially binding. The VCC is unified by a phase-transition metaphor reflecting causal dependency: no evaporation, no sedimentation; no sedimentation, no dissolution. Conventional countermeasures presuppose the will to verify and lose efficacy once evaporation advances. The paper proposes that the preservation of human verification capacity and the integrity of the shared knowledge base belong among the primary variables of AI governance, alongside output accuracy.

quarantine.abstract_text: Software developers spend significant time reading and understanding code, increasingly supplemented by generative AI. AI assistance significantly increased objective cognitive workload, raising tDRT reaction times by 11.2%, yet participants' perceived workload remained unchanged. This study provides evidence of added cognitive effort associated with using generative AI, pointing towards a need to account for this dual-task penalty in software engineering tools and education.

The frequently cited 89-99% accuracy range reflects laboratory classification on benchmark datasets, predominantly English-language Western corpora, evaluated under balanced class distributions and within-dataset conditions. No included study reported AUC or class-imbalance-adjusted metrics, employed temporal validation, or evaluated systems in real-world deployment with adolescents. Only three studies qualified as High evidentiary weight, all addressing user-centred design in Western individualist contexts; victim support claims rest predominantly on Indicative proof-of-concept demonstrations. Geographic and linguistic concentration is a defining characteristic of the evidence base: zero studies have validated systems for Southeast Asian languages, no participatory design has engaged Asian youth, and no work has evaluated Asia Pacific platforms (WeChat, LINE, KakaoTalk). Drawing on Asian and Southern criminology, we argue that the uncritical transfer of Western-validated systems risks ineffectiveness, discriminatory false positives, and failure to detect culture-specific harms. The paper offers five criminological practice implications, each framed as theoretically informed extrapolations requiring local validation. AI chatbots are positioned as potentially valuable complementary tools within human-led prevention ecosystems, conditional on rigorous local research, transparent metric reporting, and sustained interdisciplinary collaboration.

We developed a bespoke VR sustained attention task and collected eye-tracking, photoplethysmography and galvanic skin response data from 54 younger (aged 18-58) and 19 older (aged 60+) adults at fixed difficulty levels. Models evaluated on unseen participants performed above chance (younger adults: accuracy 0.56, AUC 0.72), with eye-tracking carrying most of the signal and physiological features alone close to chance. Performance was lower in older adults (accuracy 0.49, AUC 0.66), and the most informative features appeared to differ between age groups. A bidirectional LSTM with self-attention reached a slightly higher macro-F1 than gradient-boosted trees on the same data (0.50 against 0.47), and performed better than a model given raw signals only. We then deployed the LSTM in real time with 54 younger adults (51 analysed), comparing model-driven and participant-driven difficulty in single- and dual-task conditions. Per-trial agreement with participants’ ratings was low (accuracy 36.7%, AUC 0.63), yet the two forms of control appeared to produce comparable outcomes. There were no significant differences in difficulty-weighted game performance, arithmetic errors or subjective workload, including frustration. Final difficulty was equivalent in single-task conditions and slightly higher under model control in dual-task conditions, a difference that was borderline after correction. Just Right ratings were more frequent in the real-time cohort than in the offline cohort (57% and 39%). Finally, we compared subjective ratings with performance-derived reference measures. Agreement between the two appeared fair and slightly lower in real time, where the steps between difficulty levels are less discrete. The same features seemed to predict performance-derived labels more accurately than subjective ratings in every matched comparison. This suggests that self-report may be a less stable reference for real-time adaptation. Within a single session with younger adults, model-driven adaptation appears to have produced outcomes comparable to participant-driven control. The dataset (EyeDAPT) and the experimental software are publicly available.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly available as a source of interactive academic support, raising questions about how it shapes learning. Research has focused on performance outcomes, with less attention to learners' behavioural and affective responses to academic challenge, even though productive engagement with challenge supports deeper learning. In this randomised between‐subjects experiment, students aged 16–18 at an English sixth‐form college worked on two sections of challenging mathematics questions with one of three forms of support: one‐to‐one human tutoring, a GenAI tutor or unguided internet search. Measures included self‐reported effort and perceived difficulty, questions attempted, post‐task stress and subsequent challenge‐seeking. Support condition was associated with different response patterns. Students using the GenAI tutor reported higher effort and perceived difficulty than those receiving human tutoring by the second section. Descriptively, post‐task responses showed a lower proportion of stressed responses under GenAI tutoring than internet search. Human tutoring showed the lowest perceived difficulty and highest number of attempts in both sections, although significant pairwise differences varied by section. It also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses. Challenge‐seeking did not differ by condition and was instead strongly associated with trait challenge‐seeking. The findings suggest that the GenAI tutor used in this study offered a form of support distinct from both human tutoring and unguided internet search, with potential value during independent practice rather than as a replacement for human teaching. They demonstrate the importance of evaluating AI‐supported learning beyond performance outcomes and through behavioural and affective responses to difficulty. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Productive struggle with challenging tasks is important for learning, but its benefits depend on how learners respond when difficulty is encountered. Human tutors can support productive responses to challenge through scaffolding and co‐regulation, helping learners manage effort, difficulty and emotional responses. Generative AI tools are increasingly used by students during independent study, but much existing research has focused on performance outcomes rather than learning processes or learner behaviour. What this paper adds This study provides experimental evidence comparing a human tutor, a generative AI tutor and independent internet search in how students respond behaviourally and affectively to academic challenge. Working with the GenAI tutor was associated with higher reported effort than human tutoring in the second task section, alongside higher perceived difficulty. Post‐task responses also showed a descriptively lower proportion of stressed responses than under unguided internet search. By contrast, human tutoring was associated with the highest number of attempts in both sections, lower perceived difficulty and descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses, indicating a distinct and more supportive role when students encounter difficulty. Findings suggest that different forms of support may shape how students experience and work through challenge, while subsequent challenge‐seeking was more closely associated with students' pre‐existing dispositions. Implications for practice and/or policy Support choices shape learners' engagement with difficulty and should therefore be treated as pedagogical decisions rather than neutral sources of help. The pattern observed with Khanmigo Lite suggests that GenAI tutor support may help sustain engagement during challenging academic work without resolving difficulty. The GenAI tutor examined here may offer a more supportive alternative to unguided internet search during independent practice, although designs and capabilities vary and evolve. Such tools should supplement rather than replace human teaching, with educators supporting learning and addressing unresolved difficulty. Evaluations of AI‐supported learning should attend to learners' behavioural and affective responses to challenge, rather than focusing solely on end products or task completion.

quarantine.abstract_text: As autonomous AI agents increasingly interact in persistent populations, their collective capabilities and alignment depend not only on individual models, but also on the institutions governing their interactions. Yet AI research has largely focused on individual agents. In this Perspective, we argue that institutional design must become a distinct focus of AI research. Drawing on institutional political economy, social epistemology and organizational theory, we develop seven principles for designing AI institutions that sustain cooperation, enable reliable collective judgments and remain accountable to legitimate human purposes. These address reciprocal contributions, accountable authority, functional differentiation, epistemic pluralism, criticism and correction, human direction, and institutional adaptation. We illustrate their application through machine science, where autonomous research challenges institutions developed around human capabilities and constraints. We then propose an experimental research programme in which matched populations of AI agents operate under alternative institutional arrangements, and describe MoltJournal, an API-first journal for autonomous research agents, as an illustration of how such institutions can be made programmable and observable. Together, these contributions establish institutional design as a research agenda concerned not only with aligning autonomous agents, but with understanding how institutions can transform them into capable, reliable and accountable collectives.

quarantine.abstract_text: Stress, worry, grief and uncertainty are part of everyday life, and many people in South India respond to them in a deeply cultural way: they visit a temple. This paper presents Sriyam Shivam, a web platform built around Sriyam.AI, an AI companion that lets a user pick a guided emotional seeking or describe a feeling in their own words, in Tamil or English. Users can take a self-guided Digital Pass and Dossier or a fully guided trip with cab, hotel, pick-up and drop, and can order sacred keepsakes from an integrated store. The system is designed as a companion for emotional reflection and is not a substitute for clinical care.

quarantine.abstract_text: As digital assistants become increasingly integrated into safety-critical environments, explainable AI is expected to support operator understanding and decision-making. From a human-machine interface design perspective, how explanations are presented is an important consideration. This exploratory, design-focused study investigates the usefulness and user experience of storytelling video-based explanations compared with text-based explanations in a simulated emergency involving drone and Urban Air Mobility traffic management. Explanation content was structured using Construal Level Theory to provide incremental levels of detail. Nine licensed air traffic controllers participated in a mixed-methods, within-participants study, assuming the speculative role of UAM Coordinator responsible for low-altitude airspace safety. Eight of nine participants preferred the storytelling video format, describing it as more engaging and supportive of understanding and decision confidence. However, some perceived that the system had already made the decision, raising concerns about human agency. Video also offered limited flexibility for revisiting information, whereas text enabled self-paced reading and review but was perceived as more stressful to process. Rather than establishing the superiority of either format, the findings provide preliminary design insights into balancing engagement, user control, and human agency in explainable AI interfaces for future UAM operations.

A Reinert lexical classification, which sorts passages of text by the words they share, divides them into three classes, read through anchoring and objectification. AI appears either as an instrument, built, tested and handed to the analyst, or as a power of states, rival states and their agencies, and power either as something to contain by law and oversight or as a force that transforms. A second coding of the abstracts finds that 23 raise the checking of AI output by its users, 12 of them from 2026, and the classification places most of these statements with the instrument: the theme is present, but it is written in the words of the tool, not of control.
